title: Tooth structure & the dental tissues
blurb: Enamel, dentine, pulp and cementum: what each is made of and why it matters chairside.
question: A patient is surprised the dentist found decay, because the tooth has never hurt. The dentist explains the decay is still confined to the outermost layer of the crown. Which tissue is affected, and why is it painless?

teach.body: Every tooth is built from four tissues. Three are hard and mineralised (enamel, dentine and cementum) and one is soft: the pulp at the centre. Enamel covers the crown, cementum covers the root, dentine forms the bulk of the tooth underneath both, and the pulp sits inside the dentine carrying the tooth's nerves and blood supply.

teach.caption: The crown is the part above the gum, covered in enamel; the root sits in the socket, covered in cementum. They meet at the cemento-enamel junction (CEJ).
Cementum (~45–50% mineral, made by cementoblasts) covers the root and anchors the periodontal ligament fibres.

items.label: enamel is mineral, the hardest tissue in the body
dentine is mineral, with collagen and fluid-filled tubules

teach.caption: The mineral in all three hard tissues is hydroxyapatite (calcium phosphate). Fluoride can swap into it to form the more acid-resistant fluorapatite.

teach.body: Enamel has no nerves, blood supply or living cells: the ameloblasts that make it are lost once the tooth erupts. So caries confined to enamel is usually painless, and enamel can never regrow. It can, however, remineralise when fluoride and saliva redeposit mineral into an early lesion. Once decay reaches dentine, the fluid in the dentinal tubules transmits stimuli to the pulp, and the tooth becomes sensitive.

teach.caption: The pulp chamber continues down each root as a root canal, opening at the apical foramen.

items: Formative: odontoblasts lining the pulp keep making dentine throughout life.
Nutritive: blood vessels entering through the apical foramen feed the tooth.
Sensory: its nerves can only signal one thing: pain.
Defensive: it lays down tertiary (reparative) dentine in response to decay or wear.

teach.text: Don't mix up the cells: AMELOblasts make ENAMEL (and are gone after eruption), ODONTOblasts make DENTINE (and stay for life), CEMENTOblasts make cementum.

items: Enamel: crown covering, ~96% mineral, non-vital, cannot regrow but can remineralise.
Dentine: bulk of the tooth, ~70% mineral, tubules make it sensitive, keeps forming for life.
Pulp: soft centre with nerves and vessels entering through the apical foramen.
Cementum: covers the root and anchors the periodontal ligament.

summary: You can now name the four dental tissues, place each one in the tooth, explain what each is made of and which cells form it, and use that to explain why early enamel decay is painless while decay in dentine is not.

A.q: Which dental tissue is the hardest substance in the human body?
A.why: Enamel is about 96% mineral (hydroxyapatite), making it the hardest substance in the body.

whyNot.0: Dentine is only about 70% mineral, so it is softer than enamel.
whyNot.2: Cementum is roughly 45–50% mineral: similar to bone, and much softer than enamel.
whyNot.3: Alveolar bone is part of the supporting structures, not a tooth tissue, and is far less mineralised than enamel.

A.q: A patient feels sharp sensitivity once decay reaches the dentine. What structure in dentine makes this possible?
A.why: Dentine is full of fluid-filled dentinal tubules containing odontoblast processes, which transmit stimuli towards the pulp.

whyNot.0: Enamel rods (prisms) are the structural units of enamel, which has no nerve supply.
whyNot.2: Sharpey's fibres are periodontal ligament fibres embedded in cementum and bone; they anchor the tooth, they don't transmit sensation.
whyNot.3: The apical foramen is the opening at the root tip where vessels and nerves enter the pulp, not part of dentine.

A.q: Which cells form dentine and continue to do so throughout the life of the tooth?
A.why: Odontoblasts line the pulp and keep producing secondary dentine for life, plus tertiary dentine in response to injury.

whyNot.0: Ameloblasts form enamel and are lost once the tooth erupts.
whyNot.1: Cementoblasts form cementum on the root surface.
whyNot.3: Osteoclasts resorb (break down) bone; they don't form tooth tissue.

B.q: Through which structure do blood vessels and nerves enter the pulp?
B.why: Vessels and nerves enter the pulp through the apical foramen at the tip (apex) of each root.

whyNot.1: Pulp horns are extensions of the pulp chamber up towards the cusps, not an entry point.
whyNot.2: The CEJ is where enamel meets cementum at the neck of the tooth; it has no opening into the pulp.
whyNot.3: The gingival crevice is the shallow space between gum and tooth, outside the tooth entirely.

B.q: Which tissue covers the root and gives attachment to the periodontal ligament fibres?
B.why: Cementum covers the root; the periodontal ligament fibres embed into it on one side and into alveolar bone on the other.

whyNot.0: Enamel covers the crown, not the root.
whyNot.1: Dentine lies beneath the cementum and is not where ligament fibres attach.
whyNot.3: Alveolar bone forms the socket wall. Ligament fibres attach to it too, but it does not cover the root.

B.q: Why can a lesion confined to enamel be painless?
options: It has no nerves or living cells
Fluoride numbs the outer enamel surface
Saliva blocks pain signals from enamel
Enamel nerves only work when chewing
B.why: Enamel is non-vital (no nerves, blood supply or living cells), so decay limited to enamel usually causes no pain.

whyNot.1: Fluoride strengthens enamel against acid; it has no numbing effect.
whyNot.2: Saliva protects teeth by buffering acid; it doesn't block nerve signals.
whyNot.3: Enamel has no nerves at all, so there are none to work when chewing.

C.q: What is the main mineral that makes up enamel, dentine and cementum?
C.why: All three hard tissues are mineralised mainly with hydroxyapatite, a crystalline calcium phosphate.

whyNot.0: Calcium carbonate is found in eggshells and some antacids, not tooth tissue.
whyNot.2: Sodium fluoride is a fluoride source in toothpastes; fluoride converts hydroxyapatite to fluorapatite.
whyNot.3: Magnesium sulphate (Epsom salts) is not a structural tooth mineral.

C.q: Which statement about enamel is correct?
options: It slowly regrows once decay is removed
It can remineralise but never regenerate
It is formed by odontoblasts in the pulp
It is roughly 70% mineral by weight overall
C.why: Lost enamel can't regrow because ameloblasts are gone after eruption, but early lesions can remineralise with fluoride and saliva.

whyNot.0: Enamel cannot regrow: once it's lost, it needs restoring.
whyNot.2: Odontoblasts form dentine; ameloblasts form enamel.
whyNot.3: About 70% mineral describes dentine; enamel is about 96%.

C.q: Which is NOT a function of the dental pulp?
options: Nourishing the tooth through its blood vessels
Sensing hot and cold as distinct feelings
Defending against decay with new dentine
C.why: Pulp nerves can only register pain: whatever the stimulus, the patient feels it as pain rather than distinct hot or cold sensations.

whyNot.0: Producing dentine is the pulp's formative function, via odontoblasts.
whyNot.1: The pulp's blood supply nourishes the tooth (its nutritive function).
whyNot.3: Laying down tertiary dentine against decay is its defensive function.

reteach.title: Think of a tooth like a peach
reteach.question: Picture a peach: a hard skin, a thick fleshy layer, and a living stone at the centre. Where does each dental tissue fit?

blocks.body: Enamel is the tough outer skin over the crown: it protects but feels nothing. Dentine is the thick layer underneath, which has tiny fluid-filled channels running to the centre, so it can feel. The pulp is the living core with nerves and blood vessels, plugged into the body through a tiny hole at the root tip. Cementum is the thin coating on the roots that the tooth's 'ropes' (the periodontal ligament) tie into.

blocks.h: How decay is felt as it goes deeper

steps.label: Dentine
steps.sub: Tubules pass stimuli in: sensitive to sweet, hot, cold

blocks.text: Hardness order, hardest first: enamel (~96%) › dentine (~70%) › cementum (~45–50%) › pulp (soft).

explain.body: The crown's protective shell. About 96% hydroxyapatite, laid down by ameloblasts before eruption. Non-vital and the hardest tissue in the body. It can't regrow, but early lesions can remineralise.

test.why: Ameloblasts form enamel and are lost once the tooth erupts.

whyNot.3: Fibroblasts form connective tissue such as the pulp and periodontal ligament.

explain.body: The bulk of the tooth, about 70% mineral. Its dentinal tubules hold fluid and odontoblast processes, so it is sensitive. Odontoblasts keep forming secondary dentine for life and tertiary dentine when irritated.

test.q: What makes dentine sensitive when it is exposed?
test.why: Fluid movement in the dentinal tubules stimulates nerves at the pulp edge, causing sensitivity.

whyNot.1: Mineral makes tissue hard, not sensitive.
whyNot.2: Fluorapatite forms in enamel exposed to fluoride and resists acid; it isn't why dentine hurts.
whyNot.3: Prisms are the building blocks of enamel, not dentine.

explain.body: Soft connective tissue in the pulp chamber and root canals, with nerves, blood vessels and lymphatics entering through the apical foramen. Its jobs: forming dentine, nourishing the tooth, sensing (pain only) and defence.

test.q: A patient says their tooth 'feels the cold'. What will the pulp nerves actually register?
test.why: Pulp nerves only register pain, whatever the stimulus.

whyNot.1: The pulp can't distinguish temperature as a separate sensation.
whyNot.2: Pressure on biting is sensed mainly by the periodontal ligament.
whyNot.3: Touch and taste are detected by the soft tissues and tongue, not the pulp.

explain.body: A thin, bone-like layer (about 45–50% mineral) over the root, made by cementoblasts. The periodontal ligament fibres embed into it, tying the tooth to the alveolar bone.

test.q: What is the main job of cementum?
options: Protecting the crown surface from acid
Producing saliva at the gum line
test.why: Cementum covers the root and gives attachment to the periodontal ligament fibres.

whyNot.2: Nerves enter through the apical foramen, not via cementum.
whyNot.3: Saliva comes from the salivary glands.
